Tomato___healthy.label: Tomato___healthy
Tomato___healthy.description: The tomato plant shows healthy foliage, vibrant green color, and no visible lesions, wilting, or pest damage.
symptoms: Vigorous green leaves without spots or holes
Firm stems and uniform growth
No leaf curl, mold, or yellowing
prevention: Maintain consistent, regular drip irrigation at the root zone
Ensure proper plant spacing for sunlight and air circulation
Regularly inspect leaves for early signs of pests or disease
Rotate crops annually to maintain healthy soil biology
Tomato___healthy.disclaimer: Continue standard crop management and routine scouting.

Tomato___Septoria_leaf_spot.label: Tomato___Septoria_leaf_spot
Tomato___Septoria_leaf_spot.description: A destructive fungal infection caused by Septoria lycopersici that starts on lower leaves and progresses upward.
symptoms: Small, circular spots with dark brown margins and gray or tan centers
Tiny black specks (fruiting bodies) in center of spots
Leaves turn yellow around spots, then wither and fall off prematurely
prevention: Remove and destroy infected lower leaves promptly
Mulch around the base of plants to prevent fungal spores splashing from soil
Avoid overhead watering; irrigate soil directly in the early morning
Practice 2-3 year crop rotation away from solanaceous crops (tomatoes, peppers, eggplants)
Tomato___Septoria_leaf_spot.disclaimer: Consult your local agricultural extension service or certified agronomist for approved organic or chemical fungicide applications.

Tomato___Bacterial_spot.label: Tomato___Bacterial_spot
Tomato___Bacterial_spot.description: Bacterial disease caused by Xanthomonas species, thriving in warm, humid, and rainy conditions.
symptoms: Small, dark brown to black water-soaked lesions on foliage
Spots may develop a distinct yellow halo
Leaves become ragged, turn yellow, and drop
Rough, scabby raised spots on fruit
prevention: Use certified disease-free seeds and transplants
Sanitize all tools, stakes, and cages between handling plants
Avoid working in fields or touching wet foliage
Ensure wide plant spacing to promote rapid leaf drying
Tomato___Bacterial_spot.disclaimer: Consult your local agricultural extension office regarding preventive copper bactericide sprays and resistant cultivar selection.

Tomato___Late_blight.label: Tomato___Late_blight
Tomato___Late_blight.description: A fast-spreading disease caused by the oomycete Phytophthora infestans, favored by cool, wet weather.
symptoms: Irregular, water-soaked pale to dark brown greasy lesions on leaves
White fungal-like fuzz on undersides of leaves in humid conditions
Stems turn dark brown to black and plants collapse quickly
Firm, dark, greasy blotches on fruit
prevention: Remove and destroy all severely infected plants immediately (do not compost)
Keep foliage dry by watering the soil directly
Maintain excellent air circulation through proper staking and pruning
Destroy volunteer tomato and potato plants from previous seasons
Tomato___Late_blight.disclaimer: Late blight spreads rapidly in moist conditions. Immediately report outbreaks to your local agricultural extension agent for region-specific containment guidance.

Cabbage___healthy.label: Cabbage___healthy
Cabbage___healthy.description: Cabbage foliage is healthy, firm, uniformly green or purple, showing robust vegetative head formation.
symptoms: Thick, waxy, uniform green leaves
No V-shaped yellow lesions or black veins
Firm head development with no rot
prevention: Provide consistent soil moisture and avoid water stress
Mulch soil to regulate temperature and retain moisture
Scout regularly for common pests like caterpillars and aphids
Practice balanced fertilization with adequate micronutrients
Cabbage___healthy.disclaimer: Continue good cultural practices and regular field monitoring.

Tomato___Spider_mites.label: Tomato___Spider_mites
Tomato___Spider_mites.description: Microscopic arachnid pests that pierce plant cells on leaf undersides, common in hot, dry, dusty weather.
symptoms: Fine yellow or white stippling (tiny dots) across upper leaf surfaces
Delicate, silky webbing on leaf undersides and leaf axils
Leaves turn bronze, dry out, become brittle, and drop
prevention: Spray undersides of leaves with strong streams of water to dislodge mites
Maintain adequate irrigation to reduce plant moisture stress
Encourage beneficial natural predators like ladybugs and predatory mites
Control dust on field paths and suppress weeds around fields
Tomato___Spider_mites.disclaimer: Contact local agricultural officers for advice on insecticidal soaps, horticultural oils, or biological control agents.

Tomato___Leaf_Mold.label: Tomato___Leaf_Mold
Tomato___Leaf_Mold.description: Fungal disease caused by Passalora fulva (Cladosporium fulvum), prominent in high humidity and polytunnels/greenhouses.
symptoms: Pale green to yellow spots with indefinite margins on upper leaf surfaces
Olive-green to velvety brown mold growth on corresponding lower leaf surfaces
Infected leaves wither, turn yellow-brown, and die prematurely
prevention: Maximize ventilation and airflow in greenhouses and dense canopies
Keep relative humidity below 85% through heating and ventilation
Avoid wetting the foliage during watering
Prune lower foliage and suckers to enhance sunlight penetration
Tomato___Leaf_Mold.disclaimer: Check with your local agricultural officer for certified resistant tomato varieties and suitable preventive sprays.

Tomato___Tomato_Yellow_Leaf_Curl_Virus.label: Tomato___Tomato_Yellow_Leaf_Curl_Virus
Tomato___Tomato_Yellow_Leaf_Curl_Virus.description: A devastating viral disease transmitted by the silverleaf whitefly (Bemisia tabaci).
symptoms: Severe upward curling and cupping of leaf margins
Pronounced yellowing (chlorosis) between veins and along leaf margins
Marked plant stunting, bushy upright growth, and small leaves
Flower abortion and severe reduction in fruit set
prevention: Control whitefly populations using yellow sticky traps and insect exclusion netting
Remove and bag infected plants as soon as symptoms appear to prevent spread
Plant certified TYLCV-resistant or tolerant hybrid cultivars
Eliminate weed hosts around field borders
Tomato___Tomato_Yellow_Leaf_Curl_Virus.disclaimer: Viruses cannot be cured once inside the plant. Seek advice from your local agricultural extension service on integrated whitefly vector management.

Soybean___Frogeye_Leaf_Spot.label: Soybean___Frogeye_Leaf_Spot
Soybean___Frogeye_Leaf_Spot.description: A fungal disease caused by Cercospora sojina, favoring warm, humid weather and frequent rains.
symptoms: Small, circular to angular spots with dark reddish-brown borders
Centers of lesions become light gray to tan, resembling a frog's eye
Multiple spots may merge, causing large dead areas and leaf shedding
prevention: Plant certified resistant soybean seed varieties
Incorporate or bury crop residue after harvest to reduce spore carryover
Rotate crops with non-host crops such as corn or sorghum for 1-2 years
Use clean tillage where soil conservation practices permit
Soybean___Frogeye_Leaf_Spot.disclaimer: Consult your agricultural advisor to assess economic threshold and fungicide recommendations if disease pressure is high.

Soybean___Downy_Mildew.label: Soybean___Downy_Mildew
Soybean___Downy_Mildew.description: Fungal-like disease caused by Peronospora manshurica, common during cool, damp, and high-humidity weather.
symptoms: Pale green to light yellow chlorotic spots on upper leaf surfaces
Spots enlarge and turn bright yellow, later grayish-brown with yellow rims
Fluffy, grayish-purple mold on the lower leaf surface under high humidity
Whitish crust may appear on seeds from severely infected pods
prevention: Select resistant soybean cultivars adapted to your region
Rotate with corn, small grains, or other non-host crops
Avoid planting overly dense rows to allow morning dew to dry quickly
Plow under or shred crop residues after harvest
Soybean___Downy_Mildew.disclaimer: Generally causes minor yield loss unless severe. Check with your agricultural extension agent for regional scouting advice.

Corn_(maize)___Common_rust_.label: Corn_(maize)___Common_rust_
Corn_(maize)___Common_rust_.description: Fungal disease caused by Puccinia sorghi, favored by cool, moist conditions and moderate temperatures.
symptoms: Small, powdery, cinnamon-brown to reddish pustules on both leaf surfaces
Pustules rupture the leaf epidermis, releasing brown powdery spores
As plants mature, pustules turn brownish-black
Severe infection causes chlorosis and premature leaf death
prevention: Plant rust-resistant hybrid corn varieties
Plant early in the season to avoid peak spore dispersal periods
Maintain balanced nitrogen and potassium soil fertility
Rotate fields with legumes or other non-grass crops
Corn_(maize)___Common_rust_.disclaimer: Consult your local agricultural extension service for hybrid resistance ratings and targeted rust treatments.

Corn_(maize)___healthy.label: Corn_(maize)___healthy
Corn_(maize)___healthy.description: Maize foliage displays uniform dark green color, upright strong blades, and robust vegetative or ear growth.
symptoms: Broad, vibrant green leaves without chlorotic streaks or pustules
Thick, sturdy stalks and healthy root anchorage
Even tassel and ear development
prevention: Conduct soil testing and apply balanced N-P-K nutrients
Ensure proper plant population and row spacing
Manage weed competition during early growth stages
Monitor soil moisture during pollination and grain fill
Corn_(maize)___healthy.disclaimer: Continue routine field scouting and standard crop management.

Corn_(maize)___Cercospora_leaf_spot Gray.label: Corn_(maize)___Cercospora_leaf_spot Gray_leaf_spot
Corn_(maize)___Cercospora_leaf_spot Gray.description: A serious foliar fungal disease caused by Cercospora zeae-maydis, favored by high humidity, overcast days, and warm weather.
symptoms: Small, tan spots with yellow halos that expand into narrow, rectangular lesions
Lesions strictly bounded by leaf veins, creating rectangular 'box-car' shapes
Lesions turn gray or tan and can coalesce to blight entire leaves
prevention: Plant corn hybrids with high genetic tolerance or resistance
Practice crop rotation with soybeans, alfalfa, or other non-host crops
Manage surface crop residue to reduce fungal survival over winter
Avoid excessive plant densities that prolong leaf wetness
Corn_(maize)___Cercospora_leaf_spot Gray.disclaimer: Seek guidance from your local agricultural extension agent regarding economic thresholds and timely fungicide application.

Corn_(maize)___Lethal_Necrosis.label: Corn_(maize)___Lethal_Necrosis
Corn_(maize)___Lethal_Necrosis.description: A severe viral disease resulting from synergistic co-infection of Maize Chlorotic Mottle Virus (MCMV) and a potyvirus (such as SCMV).
symptoms: Severe chlorotic mottling on leaves starting from leaf margins
Drying of leaf margins and tips leading to complete 'dead heart'
Severe stunting, premature plant death, failure of ear development
Small, deformed, or rotted cobs with little or no grain
prevention: Use certified virus-free seed treated against insect vectors
Strictly enforce crop-free periods and crop rotation with non-cereal crops
Control insect vectors (thrips, leaf beetles, aphids) early in the season
Immediately uproot and burn infected plants to prevent field spread
Corn_(maize)___Lethal_Necrosis.disclaimer: Maize Lethal Necrosis can cause 100% crop loss. Promptly report suspected cases to the ministry of agriculture or local extension office.

Soybean___healthy.label: Soybean___healthy
Soybean___healthy.description: Soybean foliage is clean, rich green, and showing uniform trifoliate leaf development and vigorous pod set.
symptoms: Clean, uniform trifoliate green leaves
No spots, necrotic margins, or downy mold
Strong nodulation and healthy stem development
prevention: Ensure proper seed inoculation with Bradyrhizobium bacteria
Maintain adequate soil drainage and avoid soil compaction
Monitor fields regularly for weed escapes and defoliating insects
Practice regular multi-year crop rotation
Soybean___healthy.disclaimer: Continue good cultural practices and regular field monitoring.

Cabbage___Black_Rot.label: Cabbage___Black_Rot
Cabbage___Black_Rot.description: One of the most destructive bacterial diseases of cruciferous crops, caused by Xanthomonas campestris pv. campestris.
symptoms: Distinct V-shaped yellow (chlorotic) lesions starting at the leaf margin with wide part pointing to edge
Veins within the yellow area turn dark brown or distinctly black
Leaves turn yellow, wilt, become papery, and drop prematurely
Black ring in the vascular system when stem is cut crosswise
prevention: Use certified hot-water-treated, disease-free seed and clean transplants
Rotate with non-cruciferous crops for at least 3 years
Control cruciferous weeds (e.g., wild mustard) that harbor the bacteria
Avoid overhead sprinkler irrigation and working among plants while wet
Cabbage___Black_Rot.disclaimer: There is no cure once plants are infected. Remove diseased plants and consult your local agricultural extension service for sanitation and resistant varieties.
